I'm actually very impressed with market-chan. If we look at ESMT numbers today: 

> $1.58B MC
> $747M net cash, $274.7M net inventory from Q3
> $349.5M in Q3 free cash flow
Adjusted EV: $559.3M

> Q3 net income: $327M (1.2x annualized P/E)
> October net income (likely another +$96M added to balance sheet)

- "DDR2/DDR3 supply to remain constrained into 2027" 
- "ASPs to rise Q4" (consumer demand weakening)
- "2027 dividend payout ratio could be 30–50% of earnings"

So you're valuing the adj. operating business at $559M, despite them making ~$300m net income a quarter. 

Even the AI models I've double checked it with looked at these numbers with disbelief.

True, I've looked at biotech, physical AI, cybersecurity, space, and others... But I still have conviction that optics is the most compelling opportunity. 

If you look at Elon Musk $SPCX (Mesh acquisition), $MRVL (Lumentum acqusition), Samsung Electronics photonics foundry push... 

SK Hynix CPO push + PIC IP acqusitions... it's endless. 

Private VCs are still heavily pouring funds into upcoming optical companies.

Supply procurement is accelerating... from $SOI selling $1.2B in agreements, in a single quarter (from $25M revenue/quarter). To $COHR signing $20B in LTAs, to $LITE selling out of 2029 capacity. 

Actions about where the industry is heading is the biggest signal over valuations crashing.

Even if you stress test aggregate capex slowdown or accelerator flood vs. grid constraint/permitting downside:

- There's an economic incentive to improve GPU efficiency and power utilization. (eg. Lambda's CPO data suggests enough power savings to support ~4.5% more GPUs)... for power constrained DCs. 

- There's an economic incentive to reduce expensive HBM4 requirements in certain cases (eg. $MRVL estimating up to 30% savings through optical memory pooling)... for memory constrained inference. 

While for economic upside in these companies:

-> Optical networking, and their upstream materials like substrates and lasers represent a relatively small fraction of total AI cluster BOM.

-> At the same time, optical content goes up...while selling prices of that content rise nonlinearly as well (lasers 10x+ selling price from pluggable to CPO.)

In terms of the future winners: 

- Many low end players eg. 400G/800G, module assemblers etc. don't capture the same scale in economics from the NPO/CPO transitions... compared to laser suppliers, fiber array suppliers, modulator suppliers, or companies in the ELS/optical engine stacks. 

- Tracking capacity expansion is also important... but US/China supply chain birufration will improve scarcity economics of Western players (eg. China optical transceiver bans past 3.2T)

But even if aggregate AI capex slows, there's a strong economic incentive to accelerate optical deployments and to make every iota of compute more economically valuable. 

Visibility keeps increasing, demand keeps increasing, strategic value keeps increasing, while valuations crashed. NFA, but I'd personally, argue this is an opportunity. 

Extremely bullish on industry transition to light.

I'm hearing multiple things from industry executives:

1. Potential $NVDA employee exodus if Jensen doesn't come back soon.

Many senior management and engineers can easily retire after Nvidia stock appreciation over the years.

They don't need to continue working sitting on millions in equity. But they continued to work because Jensen was a visionary leader.

Under new interim CFO (former CFO), it gives an excuse for that lot of people to finally quit soon. A pay bump or hiring $ARM CEO isn't going to change that.

So you have generational talent leaving.

2. Loss of confidence in $NVDA future growth (Jensen was the moat).

What I'm hearing is that Jensen understands heavily top-down architectures, and it's this magical discretionary element that doesn't get covered in media.

When cuda, network, and $NVDA internal teams are arguing, Jensen made the final choices around heavily nuanced discretionary decision about where Nvidia + AI ecosystem ends up going:

Then everyone followed. The supply chain, capital, agreements, and faith.

You also can't suddenly replace the trust that local Taiwanese factories build with Jensen over the years if you bring in external CEOs, or even internal executives.

It was transformational bet after bet after bet after bet that Jensen made until Nvidia became a former $5T+ company.

3. $NVDA is not that technologically far ahead of others. It's not a 5 year lead, but months ahead to a year in different areas.

Jensen was accelerating all of that. Longer Jensen is gone, the longer Nvidia and its competitive ecosystem decays, beyond the current near-term roadmaps.

Nvidia's greatest moat was Jensen Huang making high-stake architectural decisions and accelerating capital, suppliers, + the industry to rally around his vision.

There's a massive loss of confidence in $NVDA with Jensen gone.

Gartner has cyber spending growth slowing to 11.2% next year.

I think that's way too low.

The outages put cyber back on everyone’s radar. The reason I think spending follows is that hackers are getting faster than the patch cycles companies still rely on. Anthropic is cutting its disclosure window for serious bugs from 90 days to 30 because another model can find the same flaw while the first vendor is still working on a fix.

So what does the extra budget buy? Finding exposed systems earlier, testing fixes faster, and containing the flaws you can’t patch without taking something critical offline. Anne Neuberger wants AI labs helping critical infrastructure operators do exactly that. I think those labs could end up capturing a meaningful slice of the cyber budget. And honestly there is a good chance that one of the biggest cyber companies of the next decade might be an AI lab.

$OSPN is one way we approached this at @AsymmetricBets_  Bets. Even if a hacker gets past the login, the bank still has to verify who approved the wire.
